details:
**Drinking the halahala poison**
During the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthan), the gods and asuras released a deadly poison called halahala that threatened to destroy the world. Shiva drank it to save creation, and it stuck in his throat (in some versions Parvati grabbed his throat to stop it from reaching his stomach), turning his throat blue. This earned him the epithet Nilakantha, "the blue-throated one."

**Beheading Ganesha**
Parvati created a boy to guard her chamber while she bathed. When the boy refused to let Shiva in, Shiva cut off his head in anger; to console the grieving Parvati, he replaced it with the head of an elephant (in some versions with Brahma's help). The boy became Ganesha, the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati.

**Nataraja**
Shiva's form as the "Lord of the Dance," famously depicted in medieval Chola bronzes. He dances within a ring of flames while trampling the dwarf Apasmara, who represents ignorance, and beats a small drum (damaru) whose rhythm creates and sustains the universe. His cosmic dance of destruction and renewal is the Tandava, whose gentler counterpart, performed by Parvati, is the Lasya.

**The Destroyer of the Trimurti**
Shiva forms the Hindu Trimurti, or triad of supreme gods, alongside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, with Shiva as the destroyer. He developed from the fierce Vedic storm god Rudra, who is honored in hymns such as the Shri Rudram.

**Third eye and the burning of Kama**
Shiva has a third eye on his forehead that can reduce things to ashes, which gives him the epithet Tryambaka. When the demon Taraka could only be killed by a son of Shiva, the love god Kama (Kamadeva) shot Shiva with an arrow to break his meditation and make him desire Parvati, and Shiva burned Kama to ashes with his third eye. The story is told in Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava, and Shiva's son Kartikeya was later born and defeated Taraka.

**Sati and Daksha's sacrifice**
Shiva's first wife Sati was the daughter of Daksha Prajapati, who despised Shiva and did not invite him to a great yajna (sacrifice). Insulted on her husband's behalf, Sati immolated herself in the sacrificial fire. The enraged Shiva and his attendants destroyed the sacrifice and beheaded Daksha, and Sati was reborn as Parvati.

**Pillar of fire**
In the Shiva Purana, Brahma and Vishnu argued over who was supreme, and Shiva appeared as an endless column of fire (the jyotirlinga) to settle the dispute. Vishnu, as a boar, dug down and admitted he could not find its base, while Brahma, as a swan, flew up and falsely claimed to have found its top. For this lie, Shiva (in his fierce form Bhairava) cut off one of Brahma's five heads.

**Nandi**
The white bull that serves as Shiva's mount (vahana) and as the gatekeeper of his home. Statues of Nandi typically face the main shrine in Shiva temples.

**Mount Kailash and Ravana**
Shiva lives with Parvati and their family atop Mount Kailash in the Himalayas. When the demon king Ravana tried to lift and uproot the mountain, Shiva pressed it down with his toe, pinning Ravana beneath it for a thousand years. Ravana sang Shiva's praises until he was released, and Shiva rewarded him with the sword Chandrahasa.

**The Ganges flowing from his hair**
When the river goddess Ganga descended from heaven, her torrent would have shattered the earth, so Shiva caught her in his matted locks and released her gently. He is therefore depicted with the Ganges flowing from his hair, which also holds a crescent moon.

**Lingam**
An aniconic, phallic stone pillar that is Shiva's most common object of worship. Devotees make offerings to it, and on Maha Shivaratri ("Great Night of Shiva") they recall the legend of a hunter who, hiding from tigers in a bilva (bael) tree, unknowingly dropped its leaves onto a lingam below and so won Shiva's favor.

**Race around the world between his sons**
Shiva and Parvati offered a prize (often a magic mango) to whichever of their sons, Kartikeya or Ganesha, could circle the world first. Kartikeya flew off on his peacock, but Ganesha simply walked around his parents, reasoning that they were his whole world, and won.

**Ardhanarishvara**
Shiva's androgynous form, in which he is fused with Parvati: the right half of the body is male (Shiva) and the left half is female (Parvati). It symbolizes the unity of the masculine and feminine principles.

**Trishula and vibhuti**
Shiva wields a trident called the trishula and is usually depicted covered in white ash, seated on an animal skin. His devotees mark their foreheads with three horizontal lines of sacred ash called vibhuti.

**Bhasmasura**
A demon who was granted the power to turn anyone to ash by placing his hand on their head, and then tried to use it on Shiva himself. Vishnu, taking the form of the enchantress Mohini, tricked Bhasmasura into imitating a dance move that placed his hand on his own head, reducing him to ash.
